newsitem.title: USA: Florida freeze likely to push vegetable prices up.
newsitem.headline: Florida freeze likely to push vegetable prices up.

text.p: The weekend cold snap that frosted most of Florida caused at least $100 million damage to the winter vegetable crop, pushing wholesale and retail prices immediately higher.

"We're looking at $100 million and climbing. We still have people in the field doing surveys that are coming into us bit by bit," said Bob Blankenship, a spokesman for the Florida state agriculture department.
Heavy losses were reported by some state farmers to their beans, squash, peppers and tomatoes, he said.
Temperatures early Sunday fell into the 20s in Miami's Dade County, surprising growers who had expected less-severe conditions.

Several growers said they had depended upon the National Weather Service forecast that called for overnight lows around 40 degrees, and didn't use water spraying equipment to coat the vegetables for insulation and protection.

Wholesale prices for winter vegetables were already rising quickly, according to Florida farmers. Green beans that survived the cold snap commanded $22 a bushel at a Dade County packing house on Monday, compared with $12 a bushel last week.
Some supermarkets in the Miami area marked up retail prices, reflecting the higher cost of produce.

It remained unclear how much of Florida's citrus crop was damaged by the unseasonably cold weekend weather. Citrus growers said the cold snap would reduce the orange juice yield, but were still calculating the impact of the freeze.
